stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Before standardized labeling rules were adopted, nutrition information on packaged foods was often ______: one brand of yogurt might list protein per cup, a second per container, and a third per 100 grams. Each figure could be perfectly correct, yet a shopper holding two containers had no direct way to compare them.
explanation: Skip the blank and read what comes after the colon. Three brands report the same nutrient in three different units, so a shopper cannot compare them. In one word, the labels did not follow a common standard. "Inconsistent" names exactly that problem: the information varied from one package to the next.

A.why: You picked a general complaint about labels without checking the example. The passage says each figure 'could be perfectly correct,' so the numbers were not wrong. The problem was that the units didn't match.

C.why: You matched the topic instead of the evidence. Grams and per-container figures sound technical, but the example never says the labels used jargon or were hard to understand. It shows labels that couldn't be compared because each used a different unit.

D.why: Every label in the example gives a protein figure, so information was not missing. The trouble was that it was reported in mismatched units, not that there was too little of it.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Many early folklorists assumed that songs passed down orally were reshaped constantly, with each singer adding or dropping verses at will. Fieldwork by folklorist Ines Varga in one mountain community, however, found its ballad singers to be strikingly ______: a song recorded from a grandmother in 1952 and the same song recorded from her grandson in 2014 differ by only three words.
explanation: The word "however" sets up a reversal of the old view that oral songs change constantly. The example after the colon shows a song that stayed almost word for word the same over 62 years. Your one-word summary should be something like "unchanging" or "preserving." "Conservative" is used here in its less common sense of resisting change and keeping things as they are, and it matches that summary.

A.why: "Inventive" describes the early folklorists' assumption, which "however" overturns. The recordings show the singers changed almost nothing, so this word reverses what the evidence shows.

B.why: Old ballads and grandparents may make "nostalgic" feel right. But the passage says nothing about the singers' feelings toward the past. It only shows that the words of the song were preserved.

D.why: This is a positive word that suits singers in general, but it doesn't name what the example shows. The example tracks one song staying the same over time, not how many songs the singers performed or composed.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Folklorist Amara Okafor found that the trickster tales she recorded in a string of coastal fishing villages were strikingly ______. Although the stories had passed by word of mouth for well over a century, tellers from three different generations recited them in nearly identical words, preserving even the order in which the tortoise insults each rival animal.
explanation: The sentence after the blank tells you what the blank means. The tales were passed along by word of mouth for more than a century, yet tellers from three generations recited them in nearly identical words. That describes stories that have not changed over time. "Stable" names exactly that quality: the tales stayed the same as they were handed down.

A.why: You picked a warm word that suits folk stories in general. The evidence says nothing about how much listeners love the tales. It only shows that the wording stayed the same across generations. "Beloved" fits the topic, but it does not name what the example shows.

C.why: You latched onto the detail about the order of the tortoise's insults and read it as a sign of complexity. That detail is there to show how exactly the tellers kept the tales unchanged, not how complicated the tales are. "Intricate" describes something the passage never claims.

D.why: "Adaptable" would mean the tales shifted to suit new tellers or settings. The passage says the reverse: generations of tellers kept nearly identical wording. You chose a word that clashes with the evidence after the blank.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Paleobotanists often describe the royal fern lineage as remarkably ______ in its anatomy. Fossilized stems of the genus preserved in Swedish rocks roughly 180 million years old, for example, show the same arrangement of water-conducting tissue, and even the same internal cell structures, that botanists observe in royal ferns growing in wetlands today.
explanation: The "for example" sentence shows what the blank means. Stems that are 180 million years old have the same tissue arrangement and cell structures as living royal ferns, so the plant's anatomy has barely changed over a very long time. In biology, "conservative" means slow to change, and that is exactly what the fossils show. Here an everyday word is being used in a less familiar sense.

A.why: This is the topic trap. A lineage that has lasted 180 million years sounds tough, so "resilient" feels right. But the example is about anatomy staying the same, not about the plant surviving hardship. Also, "resilient in its anatomy" is not a natural way to say anything. The word fits the general story but does not name what the evidence shows.

B.why: "Variable" means changing or diverse. The fossils show the same structures then and now, which is the opposite. You picked a word that reverses the evidence after the blank.

D.why: The passage mentions one fossil site and says modern royal ferns grow in wetlands. That tells you nothing about how widely the lineage is spread, and the example is about how its anatomy compares over time. "Widespread" claims something the text never supports.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Gray whales are best known for rolling onto their sides and sieving small crustaceans out of seafloor mud. Marine ecologist Rena Okafor argues, however, that this image understates how ______ the species' feeding is. Off the Oregon coast, her team recorded individual whales straining shrimp from kelp beds, gulping herring eggs clinging to eelgrass, and skimming crab larvae near the surface, sometimes switching methods within a single afternoon.
explanation: Skip the blank and read the sentence that follows it. It lists several kinds of prey and several ways of catching them, and says the whales sometimes switch methods in one afternoon. A one-word summary of that is "varied" or "adaptable," and "versatile" matches it. The word "however" tells you the blank corrects the narrow, mud-only picture of how gray whales feed, which fits too.

A.why: You picked a word that suits whale feeding in general. "Voracious" means eating a lot, but the example never mentions amounts. It shows a variety of foods and methods, not a large appetite.

C.why: You added an idea the passage never mentions. Nothing in the example is about time of year, and "within a single afternoon" points to quick switching, not a seasonal pattern.

D.why: You read past the evidence. "Deliberate" means slow or carefully planned, but the whales change methods quickly and take whatever food is available. That is closer to the opposite.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: In the silk workshops of 1820s Lyon, one hole punched out of place on a loom's pattern card could pull a thread out of line along an entire bolt. Because buyers laid panels side by side to compare them, inspectors rejected any length in which a woven motif sat even a millimeter off from its neighbor. Historian Ines Marchetti argues that this ______ standard explains why Lyon silk sold for nearly twice the price of its rivals.
explanation: "This ______ standard" refers back to what was just described. A single misplaced hole ruined a bolt, and a one-millimeter error was enough for rejection. A one-word summary is "strict about precision," and "exacting" names exactly that.

A.why: You matched the topic instead of the evidence. Silk patterns can be ornate, but the sentences describe how closely the work was checked, not how decorative it was. "Ornate" also doesn't describe a standard.

B.why: You reversed the evidence. Rejecting work for a one-millimeter error is the opposite of lenient.

D.why: You overlooked the reason the passage gives. Buyers compared panels side by side, so the standard had a clear purpose and wasn't arbitrary.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Many printmakers fill a woodblock with crosshatching, layered tones, and dense detail. Critics reviewing Dalia Ferreira's harbor series, by contrast, have singled out its ______: in one print, a single gouged line stands in for an entire shoreline, and in several others the sky is simply left as bare, uninked paper. The scenes, one reviewer noted, feel complete despite how little has been carved.
explanation: Read what comes after the colon. One line stands for a whole shoreline, skies are left blank, and the reviewer remarks on "how little has been carved." A one-word summary is "restraint." "Economy" can mean exactly that, achieving a lot with very little. "By contrast" also sets Ferreira against printmakers who pack their blocks with detail.

A.why: You picked a word that sounds like printmaking but doesn't name what the example shows. Bare paper and single lines suggest very little surface texture. Texture describes the dense blocks Ferreira is contrasted with.

C.why: You reversed the contrast. The passage says Ferreira does the opposite of filling the block, so "abundance" points the wrong way.

D.why: You read in a quality the passage never mentions. Nothing in the example is about balance or mirrored halves, only about how little is carved.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: For decades, planners in one coastal city treated its narrow back lanes as purely ______ spaces: corridors for delivery vans and trash collection, valued only for the work they made possible. That view changed after the city began licensing small cafés and shops to open onto the lanes. Within ten years, the lanes drew more evening pedestrians than several of the main streets running alongside them.
explanation: Skip the blank and read what follows the colon: the lanes were corridors for deliveries and trash, valued only for the work they made possible. One word for 'valued only for its function' is 'utilitarian.' The rest of the passage then overturns that older view, so the blank has to name the view itself, not what the lanes later became.

A.why: You picked a word that fits a passage about old city streets in general. Nothing after the colon is about age or heritage. It describes only what the lanes were used for.

C.why: You put the blank on the wrong side of the reversal. 'Communal' describes the lanes after the cafés opened, which is the finding that knocks down the planners' view. It is not the view itself.

D.why: You assumed that lanes used by delivery vans must be crowded. The explanation after the colon says nothing about traffic levels, only that the lanes were valued for their function.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Civil engineer Dalia Okoro's protocol for inspecting steel bridges is notably ______. Where a standard inspection samples roughly one bolt in twenty on a given span, her teams check every bolt and record each torque reading individually. As a result, an Okoro inspection of a single span takes about four times as long as a conventional one, but it leaves no connection unexamined.
explanation: The sentences after the blank give a concrete contrast. A standard inspection checks one bolt in twenty, while Okoro's teams check every bolt and leave no connection unexamined. The one-word summary of 'checks everything' is 'exhaustive.'

A.why: The passage says her inspections take about four times as long as conventional ones. That is the opposite of efficient.

B.why: You read more into the passage than it says. Nothing suggests the protocol is untested or still being trialled, only that it is more thorough than the standard.

C.why: You chose a generally positive word that suits an engineer's new method. It does not name the specific quality the example shows: checking every bolt instead of a sample.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Many track coaches regard a sprinter's top speed as largely ______—set mostly by genetics and only slightly improvable through training. A recent study of collegiate sprinters challenges that view. Athletes who added eight weeks of resisted-sled work to their routine raised their peak velocity by 4 percent, while a control group that did only standard drills gained less than 1 percent.
explanation: Read past the dash: the coaches' view is that top speed is 'set mostly by genetics.' One word for a quality you are born with is 'innate.' The study then challenges that view, so the blank has to state the belief before it is knocked down.

B.why: You described what the study found, not what the coaches believe. Top speed being adaptable is the conclusion that challenges the view in the blank.

C.why: You matched the topic instead of the function. Sprint speed can be measured, and the study measured it, but the phrase after the dash is about where speed comes from, not whether it can be measured.

D.why: You picked a word that fits elite sprinting in general. Nothing after the dash is about how impressive top speed is. It says only that speed is set by genetics.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Historians once assumed that eighteenth-century Indian chintz painters worked quickly and loosely, letting color fall where it might. Surviving workshop records suggest a far more ______ practice: a single cotton panel could pass through as many as eleven separate stages of mordanting, dyeing, and washing, each timed to the hour and checked against a master sample before the next stage began.
explanation: Skip the blank and read what comes after the colon. It shows eleven stages, each timed to the hour and checked against a master sample. One word for that is careful and exact. 'Meticulous' names that. The phrase 'far more' also tells you the blank is the opposite of the old view that the painters worked 'quickly and loosely.'

A.why: You matched the topic instead of the evidence. Chintz is a decorated fabric, so 'ornate' sounds right, but the colon describes how carefully the work was done, not how elaborate the design looked.

B.why: You chose the side of the reversal that gets knocked down. 'Hurried' matches the old assumption that the painters worked 'quickly and loosely,' and the records disprove it.

D.why: You added a claim the passage never makes. The records describe the steps and the checks, and nothing about profit or money.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Coaches often treat an athlete's peak heart rate during a sprint as the clearest sign of fitness. A study of collegiate rowers points to a more ______ measure: how quickly the heart rate falls in the first minute after effort ends. Rowers whose rates dropped fastest tended to post the best times late in the season, regardless of how high their rates had climbed.
explanation: Read past the colon first. The recovery measure tracks which rowers perform best, and peak heart rate does not. So the blank needs a word meaning 'informative' or 'revealing.' 'Telling' is a plain word with exactly that second meaning: it tells you something about fitness.

A.why: You matched the topic. A sprint is strenuous, but the measure is taken after the effort ends, and the word has to describe what the measure reveals, not how hard the exercise is.

B.why: You reversed the contrast. The conventional measure is the coaches' peak heart rate, and the study offers recovery rate as the alternative to it.

C.why: You chose a word that is too strong. The rowers only 'tended to' post better times, which is a hedged finding from one study and does not support calling the measure conclusive.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Early designers of suspension bridges treated wind as a static load, a steady push the deck simply had to withstand. After several decks twisted apart in only moderate breezes, engineers came to regard wind as a ______ force: gusts arriving at particular intervals could set a deck swinging, and each swing could amplify the next until the structure failed.
explanation: The explanation after the colon describes motion that changes over time: gusts at intervals and swings that build on one another. That is the opposite of the earlier 'static load.' 'Dynamic' names a force that acts through changing motion, which fits both the contrast and the example.

A.why: You chose the view the passage knocks down. A 'steady push' is the old static idea, and the new understanding is about gusts that rise and fall.

B.why: You picked a word that is true of wind in general but does not name what the colon shows. Every wind is natural. The point here is how the force varies over time.

D.why: You missed a qualifier. The decks failed in 'only moderate breezes,' so the danger came from the timing of the gusts, not their strength.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Archaeologists had long assumed that the potters of the ancient river town of Tell Qaran worked on their own, each following personal habits passed down within a family. The jars recovered from the site show a striking ______: vessels from households on opposite sides of the town are nearly indistinguishable, with wall thickness, rim width, and the spacing of incised bands matching to within a fraction of a millimeter.
explanation: Skip the blank and read what follows the colon. Jars from different households are "nearly indistinguishable" and match "to within a fraction of a millimeter." Your one-word summary is sameness, and "uniformity" names exactly that. It also overturns the earlier assumption that each family worked by its own habits.

B.why: You picked a positive word that suits pottery in general. The colon doesn't praise how well the jars were made. It shows that they are all the same, and "craftsmanship" doesn't name that.

C.why: You matched the topic, since archaeological finds are old. Nothing after the colon is about age. It's about how closely the jars match each other.

D.why: You chose the opposite of what the evidence shows. Jars that are "nearly indistinguishable" are not varied. "Variety" would fit the assumption the passage is overturning, not the finding.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: Biologists tracking a population of sea otters along the central California coast found that the animals are remarkably ______ foragers. One otter may eat almost nothing but purple sea urchins, while another diving in the same kelp bed specializes in crabs or turban snails, and each animal tends to keep its preference for years, even when its usual prey becomes harder to find.
explanation: The next sentence defines the blank. Each otter sticks to one kind of prey and keeps that preference for years, even when the prey gets scarce. Your summary is "choosy" or "selective." Here "particular" carries that less common sense of fussy about what one accepts, and it matches the example exactly.

B.why: You picked a word that goes naturally with "foragers." The example says nothing about how much the otters eat. It shows that each one eats only one kind of thing.

C.why: You read "each animal" as a sign that otters live alone. The otters in the example dive "in the same kelp bed," so they are not solitary. The passage is about diet, not company.

D.why: You chose a general compliment. Nothing in the example shows how good the otters are at catching prey. It only shows which prey each one sticks to, so "skilled" claims something the text never supports.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
stimulus: For much of the twentieth century, foresters in the southeastern United States treated fire as a ______ to longleaf pine savannas, putting out every blaze they could reach. Decades of monitoring have reversed that view: where fire was kept out, hardwood shrubs crowded out pine seedlings and the grasses that shelter wildlife, while plots burned every few years kept their open, species-rich character.
explanation: The blank belongs to the old view, the one the colon says was "reversed." The phrase "putting out every blaze they could reach" fixes it. You only suppress something you see as dangerous. "Threat" is that label, and the monitoring results then overturn it.

B.why: You matched the finding instead of the belief it overturns. Fire as a "necessity" is the corrected view. Foresters who put out every blaze clearly didn't think fire was necessary.

C.why: You chose a word that suits landscapes in general. Nothing in the passage presents fire as a line or edge. The point is whether fire harms the savanna or sustains it.

D.why: You picked a positive word, which reverses the foresters' attitude. People who put out every fire did not see it as something useful to them.
